algorithms.name: Bubble Sort
algorithms.description: Bubble Sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order, moving the largest elements to the end in each pass.
algorithms.longDescription: Bubble Sort is one of the simplest sorting algorithms. It works by repeatedly stepping through the list, comparing adjacent elements, and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. This process is repeated until the list is sorted. In each pass, the largest unsorted element 'bubbles up' to its correct position at the end of the array.
algorithms.pseudocode:
procedure bubbleSort(A: list)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 0 to n-1
        for j = 0 to n-i-1
            if A[j] > A[j+1]
                swap A[j] and A[j+1]
            end if
        end for
    end for
end procedure
advantages: Simple implementation - easy to understand and code
Works well for small datasets
Adaptive - can achieve O(n) when array is already sorted
Stable sorting algorithm - maintains the relative order of equal elements
disadvantages: Very inefficient for large datasets with O(n²) time complexity
Much slower than other sorting algorithms like Merge Sort or Quick Sort
Not suitable for real-world applications with large data
useCases: Educational purposes - to understand basic algorithm concepts
Small datasets where simplicity is more important than efficiency
When the data is nearly sorted (can achieve O(n) in this case)

algorithms.name: Selection Sort
algorithms.description: Selection Sort finds the minimum element from the unsorted part of the array and puts it at the beginning, building the sorted array one element at a time.
algorithms.longDescription: Selection Sort divides the array into a sorted and an unsorted region. It repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted region and moves it to the end of the sorted region. The algorithm maintains two subarrays: the subarray which is already sorted and the remaining subarray which is unsorted. In every iteration, the minimum element from the unsorted subarray is picked and moved to the sorted subarray.
algorithms.pseudocode:
procedure selectionSort(A: list)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 0 to n-1
        min_idx = i
        for j = i+1 to n-1
            if A[j] < A[min_idx]
                min_idx = j
            end if
        end for
        swap A[i] and A[min_idx]
    end for
end procedure
advantages: Simple implementation with minimal code
Performs the minimum possible number of swaps (n-1)
Works well when memory write is a costly operation
In-place algorithm with O(1) extra space
disadvantages: Always O(n²) time complexity even for sorted data
Not stable - relative order of equal elements may change
useCases: When minimizing the number of swaps is important
When memory write is a costly operation
For small arrays where simplicity matters more than efficiency

algorithms.name: Insertion Sort
algorithms.description: Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one element at a time, taking each element from the unsorted part and inserting it into its correct position within the sorted part.
algorithms.longDescription: Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. It takes each element from the unsorted portion and inserts it into its correct position in the sorted portion. The algorithm iterates through the array, and for each element, it compares it with the previous elements in the sorted portion and shifts elements greater than the current one to the right until it finds the correct position.
algorithms.pseudocode:
procedure insertionSort(A: list)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 1 to n-1
        key = A[i]
        j = i-1
        while j >= 0 and A[j] > key
            A[j+1] = A[j]
            j = j-1
        end while
        A[j+1] = key
    end for
end procedure
advantages: Simple implementation with minimal code
Efficient for small datasets
Adaptive - efficient for nearly sorted arrays with O(n) time
Stable algorithm - maintains relative order of equal elements
In-place algorithm with O(1) extra space
Online algorithm - can sort a list as it receives it
disadvantages: O(n²) time complexity in average and worst cases
Requires many element shifts for insertions
useCases: Small datasets where simplicity matters
Nearly sorted arrays (adaptive behavior gives O(n) performance)
Online data streams where elements come one at a time
As part of more complex algorithms (like in quick sort for small subarrays)

algorithms.name: Merge Sort
algorithms.description: Merge Sort uses the divide-and-conquer approach, splitting the array in half, recursively sorting each half, and then merging the sorted halves back together.
algorithms.longDescription: Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and then merges the sorted halves to produce a sorted output. The key operation is the merging of two sorted subarrays. During the merge, the algorithm compares elements from both subarrays and places them in the correct order in a temporary array, which is then copied back to the original array.
algorithms.pseudocode:
procedure mergeSort(A: list, start, end)
    if start < end
        mid = (start + end) / 2
        mergeSort(A, start, mid)
        mergeSort(A, mid+1, end)
        merge(A, start, mid, end)
    end if
end procedure

procedure merge(A: list, start, mid, end)
    create temp arrays L and R
    copy A[start..mid] to L
    copy A[mid+1..end] to R
    
    i = 0, j = 0, k = start
    while i < size(L) and j < size(R)
        if L[i] <= R[j]
            A[k] = L[i]
            i = i + 1
        else
            A[k] = R[j]
            j = j + 1
        end if
        k = k + 1
    end while
    
    copy remaining elements of L or R
end procedure
advantages: Efficient with guaranteed O(n log n) time complexity in all cases
Stable algorithm - maintains relative order of equal elements
Parallelizable - different parts can be sorted in parallel
Works well for large datasets and linked lists
disadvantages: Requires O(n) extra space for the temporary arrays during merging
Slower for small arrays compared to insertion sort
useCases: When stable sorting is needed
When guaranteed O(n log n) performance is required
For external sorting (when data doesn't fit in memory)
When parallel processing is available

algorithms.name: Quick Sort
algorithms.description: Quick Sort selects a 'pivot' element and partitions the array around it, with smaller elements to the left and larger ones to the right, then recursively sorts both partitions.
algorithms.longDescription: Quick Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that selects a 'pivot' element from the array and partitions the other elements into two sub-arrays according to whether they are less than or greater than the pivot. The algorithm selects a pivot, partitions the array around it (elements smaller than the pivot go to the left, larger to the right), and then recursively sorts the sub-arrays. The pivot selection and partitioning strategy greatly affect the algorithm's performance.
algorithms.pseudocode:
procedure quickSort(A: list, low, high)
    if low < high
        pivotIndex = partition(A, low, high)
        quickSort(A, low, pivotIndex - 1)
        quickSort(A, pivotIndex + 1, high)
    end if
end procedure

procedure partition(A: list, low, high)
    pivot = A[high]
    i = low - 1
    
    for j = low to high - 1
        if A[j] <= pivot
            i = i + 1
            swap A[i] with A[j]
        end if
    end for
    
    swap A[i + 1] with A[high]
    return i + 1
end procedure
advantages: Very efficient with O(n log n) average-case time complexity
In-place algorithm with low memory overhead
Cache-friendly with good locality of reference
Performs well in practice for most real-world data
disadvantages: O(n²) worst-case time complexity with bad pivot choices
Not stable - relative order of equal elements may change
Performance depends on the pivot selection strategy
useCases: When average-case performance is important
When memory usage is a concern
For general-purpose sorting in most applications
When in-place sorting is required

algorithms.name: Heap Sort
algorithms.description: Heap Sort builds a max-heap from the array and repeatedly extracts the maximum element, placing it at the end of the array and reconstructing the heap.
algorithms.longDescription: Heap Sort uses a binary heap data structure to sort elements. It first builds a max heap (where parent nodes are greater than or equal to their children), and then repeatedly extracts the maximum element from the heap and rebuilds the heap. The algorithm works in two phases: first, it builds a max heap from the input array; second, it repeatedly removes the largest element from the heap (the root) and places it at the end of the array, then restores the heap property.
algorithms.pseudocode:
procedure heapSort(A: list)
    n = length(A)
    
    // Build max heap
    for i = n/2-1 down to 0
        heapify(A, n, i)
    end for
    
    // Extract elements from heap
    for i = n-1 down to 0
        swap A[0] with A[i]
        heapify(A, i, 0)
    end for
end procedure

procedure heapify(A: list, n, i)
    largest = i
    left = 2*i + 1
    right = 2*i + 2
    
    if left < n and A[left] > A[largest]
        largest = left
    end if
    
    if right < n and A[right] > A[largest]
        largest = right
    end if
    
    if largest != i
        swap A[i] with A[largest]
        heapify(A, n, largest)
    end if
end procedure
advantages: Guaranteed O(n log n) time complexity in all cases
In-place algorithm with O(1) extra space
No worst-case scenarios like in Quick Sort
Efficient for finding the k largest (or smallest) elements
disadvantages: Not stable - relative order of equal elements may change
Poor cache performance due to scattered memory access patterns
Often slower than Quick Sort in practice despite same time complexity
Relatively complex implementation compared to other algorithms
useCases: When worst-case guarantee of O(n log n) is needed
When memory usage is a concern (in-place sorting)
As part of applications that already use heap data structures
When stable sorting is not required
